summary.text: The closed issue reports that upgrading from HTTPX 0.28.1 to the 1.0.dev1 pre-release removed the top-level `httpx.BaseTransport` attribute. A project member confirmed that the pre-release was intentionally available on PyPI, but the retrieved discussion does not establish whether this API removal itself was intentional or identify a migration path.

known_facts.text: The reporter installed the latest pre-release with `uv pip install -U --pre httpx` and then received an `AttributeError` when accessing `httpx.BaseTransport`; Python suggested `Transport`.
The reporter stated that the behavior appeared after upgrading from the latest stable version to the published development version.
Another contributor noted that the PyPI description for 1.0.dev1 did not provide information about the release.
On July 14, 2025, project member lovelydinosaur confirmed that a 1.0 pre-release was available on PyPI and said they would discuss it further soon, linking to a GitHub discussion.
The issue was closed on July 14, 2025, but closure alone does not establish that `BaseTransport` was restored, documented, or given a migration path.

missing_information: Whether removal of the top-level `BaseTransport` export was an intentional 1.0 API change or an unintended packaging/export regression.
What supported replacement or migration path was intended for code that depended on `httpx.BaseTransport`.
Whether later documentation or releases addressed the change; current source code, release notes, and package contents were not inspected.
content.draft_reply: Thanks for documenting the upgrade path and exact exception. This showed that moving from 0.28.1 to 1.0.dev1 removed the top-level `httpx.BaseTransport` export. On July 14, 2025, lovelydinosaur confirmed that the 1.0 pre-release was intentionally available on PyPI and said more information would follow, but the discussion captured here did not clarify whether this particular API removal was intentional or whether `Transport` was a compatible replacement. Anyone revisiting this should consult the current 1.0 API and migration documentation rather than assuming the suggested `Transport` name is a drop-in replacement; the intended replacement and migration path should be documented explicitly.
limitations: No repository source code, package artifacts, release notes, PyPI content, or linked GitHub discussion was inspected, so the current API and eventual resolution are unknown.
Two repository searches for `BaseTransport` with `1.0.dev1` or `missing` produced no eligible comparison candidates. Those searches do not rule out duplicates phrased differently.
The complete two-comment thread was retrieved, but it contains no explicit maintainer determination about whether the missing export was intentional.

sources.title: httpx.BaseTransport dropped from 0.28.1 to 1.0.dev1
sources.excerpt:
Reproduce:

```shell
uv pip install -U --pre httpx
python
```

```python
import httpx
```
```python
httpx.BaseTransport
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<input>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: module 'httpx' has no attribute 'BaseTransport'. Did you mean: 'Transport'?
```

This happens after upgrading from the latest stable version to the published dev version

issue.title: Pytest can't handle custom classes in parameterized tests (major bug).
issue.author: ketchupee1

summary.text: The report concerns parametrized test collection failing while pytest generates an automatic parameter ID for a custom mapping-like instance whose attribute lookup raises KeyError for __name__. The maintainer discussion treated that instance behavior as incompatible with normal attribute lookup and recommended an explicit parameter ID rather than a pytest change.

known_facts.text: The reported traceback originates in _idval_from_value while pytest evaluates getattr(val, "__name__", None), which raises KeyError.
The reporter clarified that the custom class overrides __getattr__ and __setattr__, and said the same tests had worked roughly one week earlier without changes to the test script.
The reporter said converting the custom object to a normal dict avoids the failure, and later described a workaround that changes the custom attribute-access behavior for undefined attributes.
A maintainer requested a minimal reproducer and explained that an instance whose __getattr__ raises KeyError is the problematic case; explicit parametrization IDs were recommended.
The concrete workaround provided in the discussion was pytest.param(MyBroken(), id="broken").
The issue is closed and currently carries the status: needs information label, but the closed state alone does not establish that pytest code was changed or a fix was released.

missing_information: A minimal standalone reproducer containing the custom class and its __getattr__/__setattr__ implementations.
The exact pytest versions from the last working and first failing environments, plus whether Python or other dependencies changed during that interval.
The complete traceback and parametrization declaration, including whether an explicit id avoids the failure in the reporter's actual test.
content.draft_reply:
Thanks for the additional explanation. The failure occurred while pytest was deriving an automatic ID for the parameter value: it queried `__name__`, and the instance’s custom attribute lookup raised `KeyError`. As discussed above, missing attributes should not escape from `__getattr__` as `KeyError`; the instance can instead raise `AttributeError` for an unknown attribute.

For an object that intentionally keeps that behavior, the supported workaround is to provide the test ID explicitly rather than modify pytest internals:

```python
pytest.param(MyBroken(), id="broken")
```

The report did not include a minimal reproducer or the exact pytest versions before and after the reported change, so it was not possible from this discussion to establish a pytest regression. If this is revisited, please include the smallest custom class and parametrized test that demonstrate it, along with the last working and first failing pytest versions.
limitations: Only the first page of discussion was retrieved: 10 of 11 reported comments. Two retrieved comment excerpts were omitted from the available evidence, so their contents were not inferred.
The repository's source code, release history, and runtime behavior were not inspected or tested; no root cause, code change, or released fix was independently verified.

The issue search returned candidate issues, including one about parametrization IDs for classes without __name__, but no candidate's full content was available for comparison. Therefore, the recorded search does not establish or rule out a duplicate.

sources.title: Pytest can't handle custom classes in parameterized tests (major bug).
sources.excerpt:
Hello.

I'm having an issue with Pytest where I'm unable to run parameterized tests with custom class objects. 

Script path: ...\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python314\Lib\site-packages\_pytest\python.py
Lineno: 1052

Error:  
```
1052: in _idval_from_value
    elif isinstance(getattr(val, "\_\_name\_\_", None), str):
                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
E   KeyError:  '\_\_name\_\_'
-------------------------------------
```

I should note that on my side, the test that now is unable to run had passed before about one week ago,  and nothing has changed within the test script itself. 

It seems to be that my custom class, which is basically a wrapper around the Python Dict builtin class, causes the error to now raise, whereas if I convert this to a normal python Dict, the tests passes again.

sources.excerpt:

This doesn't really makes sense, if the class itself works for something, the class instance should work for that same something since it's easy to derive the class from the instance. Plus the same tests worked without any modifications, so the problem must be on Pytest's end.

I actually made a work around where I simply changed the default getattr and setattr behaviour if the attribute in question wasn't already defined. I still used the same instance as before, and nothing else had changed.

issue.title: new rule: lazy import used at top level
issue.author: KotlinIsland

summary.text: The report requests a lint rule for a PEP 810 lazy import that is referenced at module scope, thereby resolving it during module loading. The issue is closed, and the sole comment links the existing `lazy-import-immediately-resolved` rule documentation.

known_facts.text: The supplied example uses `lazy import amongus` and then assigns the imported name to a module-level variable; the reporter says this largely defeats the purpose of a lazy import.
A contributor responded with a link to Ruff's `lazy-import-immediately-resolved` rule documentation.
Earlier issue #25014 proposed warning when names created by lazy imports are used at unconditional module scope or in an immediately nested class body.
The target issue was opened and closed on October 7, 2026, and has no labels.

content.draft_reply: Thanks for the concise example. This case appears to be covered by the existing `lazy-import-immediately-resolved` rule linked above. The earlier proposal in #25014 explicitly included lazy-imported names used at unconditional module scope, which matches the assignment shown here. The recommendation is therefore to use that existing rule rather than add a separate diagnostic.
limitations: The linked rule documentation, Ruff source code, tests, and releases were not inspected, so present implementation details and version availability were not independently verified.
Only the title and body of candidate issue #25014 were available; its comments and any linked implementation were not reviewed.
The search returned three candidates, but only the most directly relevant candidate was read in full.

comparisons.reason: Both issues request detection of a lazy-imported name being used at module scope and therefore resolved during module loading. The earlier proposal expressly includes global-scope uses, making the target's assignment example a concrete instance of its requested behavior.
similarities: Both concern PEP 810 lazy imports that are resolved during module loading.
Both seek a lint diagnostic for use of a lazy-imported name at module scope.
Both describe the behavior as contrary to the apparent intent of declaring the import lazy.
differences: The target demonstrates a direct module-level assignment, while #25014 illustrates a module-level class inheriting from the imported name.
Issue #25014 discusses broader scope boundaries and whether an autofix would be appropriate; the target does not address those design details.

sources.title: Lint against PEP 810 lazy imports that would be immediately resolved
sources.excerpt:
Title: Lint against PEP 810 lazy imports that would be immediately resolved
State: closed

### Summary

With the new PEP-810 lazy imports in Python 3.15, it's possible to write code like this:

```python
lazy import foo

class Bar(foo.Foo): ...
```

where the "lazy" import gets resolved immediately at module load time. That isn't what the user intended, so linters should warn against it.

The rule should check for names created through a lazy import and used either in the module global scope (and not within an except block or conditional block) or in a class body that is immediately within the global scope. More ambitiously, we could also check function bodies that we detect are called directly from the module scope (e.g. decorators, dataclass annotations). Doing this in full generality is obviously intractable, but some heuristics could go a long way.

I'm not sure the rule should have an autofix. Removing "lazy" is an obvious solution, but it may not be what the user wants: if they wrote `lazy` they probably intended it to be lazy, and we should give them a chance to fix their code.
